newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Weak results dull interest in S.Africa gold shares.
newsitem.headline: Weak results dull interest in S.Africa gold shares.

text.p: Lacklustre third quarter gold results have done nothing to rekindle investment in South African gold shares, already on the wane due to a sickly bullion price, analysts and dealers said on Monday.

The all-gold index has lost nearly five percent on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange since last Monday when Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd kicked off the reporting round with earnings slashed by a third in the September quarter.
"We have had four sets of results and not one was impressive...There is more value elsewhere than in golds," one share dealer said of the market decline.
Although Gencor Ltd managed to slightly raise earnings, profits at Anglovaal Ltd and Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd both dipped on the preceding quarter.

In the first half of 1996 South African gold mines were sheltered to a large degree by the fall in the rand which boosted the local currency income they received for their metal. But since mid-year the rand's decline has slowed while the dollar price of bullion has come under pressure.

The yellow metal spiked up to nearly $420 an ounce at the start of the year but has been in steady decline since then, breaking below the key $380 support level at the end of last month. It was hovering around $380 on Monday.

Besides worries over a feeble metal price, analysts said the gold share market was spooked by still declining South African gold output, recent mine violence and increased working costs due to wage increases which took effect from July 1.
"Firstly the gold price is sloppy -- but secondly the reports of violence and trouble have frightened people and they'd rather sit and wait until it finishes and see what happens," one analyst said.

Others agreed that in the absence of the necessary incentives -- a firmer bullion price and improved output, feeding through into higher profits -- investors would remain unenthusiastic about gold shares.

"We haven't had the ingredients there to make people aggressive buyers of golds. We need to see productivity improvement. All the companies that have reported this last week have shown a decline in productivity," another analyst said.
With anxiety about the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and some central banks selling their gold reserves still hanging over the gold market, the onus is on mines to improve their investor image.
"We need to see improvement in all the companies otherwise the index is not going anywhere," said Dean Cunningham, analyst at Investec Securities.
